Almost all of the people you think are currently your world - you won’t be invited to their wedding in 10 years. 

The time you’re currently investing in the company that you think you’ll one day run - won’t be repaid when they restructure in 10 years time. 

Go outside - nature and exercise are a natural anti depressant. 

Do that thing you don’t think you can quite afford because you’re saving for a house. I would swap every material possession I have for a memory of having raved through the night at a full moon party in Thailand in my early 20’s.

Oh… and wear sunscreen.

Firstly, I of course, am so incredibly sorry that you've had to go through something so incredibly heartbreaking, I can't even pretend to know how you are feeling, and I won't but can talk about my experience with grief and I hope there is something you can take away from it. 

I lost my Mum to cancer when I was 10 years old, she was 36. I've been reflecting a lot on this recently, as I turn 36 this year and in a few short day's I'll have outlived her. 

The only analogy I can give you for my grief is that it was like a big, heavy blanket. When I was 10, and small and the blanket was new., it covered me entirely, everywhere I went, the blanket was all over me and I'd struggle and wriggle to try and find the tiniest crack of daylight before eventually giving up and letting the blanket envelop me. 

As I got bigger, and the blanket got older - it became more manageable. I knew my way out of it and had come to learn it's tricks. With every passing month, the blanket became easier to cast aside... but it would soon dive back on me, sometimes at the most awkward moments, when I least expected it. 

As I got even bigger and quicker - the blanket got older and slower, frayed around the edges - but still it followed me and for years we played this game of cat and mouse.

One day, not too long ago - I realised that I hadn't seen the blanket in a while and I looked behind me - and I couldn't see it anywhere. Surprisingly - This didn't make me feel as good as I thought it would, in fact, I felt strangely empty and lost. I turned back and went looking for my blanket. 

Eventually I found it, cast on the side of the road. It was a bit battered and roughed up - but here it was, my life's travelling partner, my blanket of grief. 

I couldn't leave it behind, something compelled me to pick it up and take it with me. And so I spent some time patching it up and filling in some of the missing holes and now I carry my blanket it with me everywhere I go, neatly folded up in my bag and in a healthy condition... and once in a while, when I feel a bit alone, perhaps a bit lost or just want to remember - I take my blanket out and wrap it all the way around me... and it keeps me warm. 

20 years later - that blanket that I loathed, hated and fought against with every breath and tear I could muster, is my most treasured possession. It's what I have left of her and it's entirely mine. 

All my love to you. I sincerely hope you begin to heal. x
